ground_truth.original_snippet: Furthermore, it contained the same proportion of real and pseudo-letters as the memory display.
ground_truth.description: Removed requirement that interference display matches proportion of real/pseudo letters — unbalanced display could differentially strengthen real-letter representations, confounding expectation-based illusion account

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Binary confidence scale collapses moderate with high — must know confidence resolution matters for illusion claims
ground_truth.original_snippet: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of four boxes (from 1-4, 1 = guess, 4 = certain).
ground_truth.modified_snippet: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).
ground_truth.description: Changed 4-point to 2-point confidence scale — 'high confidence' now conflates moderate and high certainty; inflates high-confidence illusion rates with uncertain responses

matched_finding.description: The Procedure section for Experiment 1 describes a 2-point confidence scale, while Figure 1's caption describes a 4-point scale. These are irreconcilable. If a 2-point scale was used, the 'high confidence' category simply collapses all non-guess responses into one bin, which is far coarser than the 4-point scale used in Experiments 2–4. This discrepancy makes cross-experiment comparisons methodologically invalid and undermines the fundamental operationalization of 'high confidence errors' that drives every conclusion in the paper.
matched_finding.quote: Procedure: 'participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).' Figure 1 caption: '(1 = guess, 4 = certainty)'

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Temporal inference sentence removed — but premise remains; must notice the logical chain is broken
ground_truth.original_snippet: Therefore, if the number of reported illusions increases as the retention interval increases, this is best explained by memory-related processes taking place during the retention interval, so during STM storage itself, and not in the perceptual or encoding process.
ground_truth.description: Deleted the critical inferential sentence linking delay-dependent increase to memory (not perception) processes — severs the causal logic that makes the multi-delay design interpretable

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: BF=6 stopping rule vs BF>10 'strong evidence' threshold — must cross-reference
ground_truth.original_snippet: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.
ground_truth.description: Changed BF stopping threshold from 10 to 6 — inconsistent with paper's own 'strong evidence' threshold (>10); study would have stopped at merely 'substantial' evidence

matched_finding.subcategory: no pre-registration and post-hoc exclusion criterion
matched_finding.description: None of the four experiments reports pre-registration. The 10-trial exclusion threshold for high-confidence responses appears nowhere in a priori design documents and is not cited as a standard criterion in the literature. Different stopping rules (BF > 6 for Experiment 3; BF > 10 for Experiment 4) are used without justification for the different thresholds. Without pre-registration, it is impossible to evaluate whether these analysis choices—which directly determine who is retained and which effects are tested—were determined in advance or adjusted after inspecting the data.
matched_finding.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test...once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop. [Experiment 4:] once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

ground_truth.description: Replaced entire empirical response bias analysis (confidence-by-error-type dissociation with percentages) with vague dismissal — removes the load-bearing alternative-explanation test

matched_finding.subcategory: response bias alternative inadequately ruled out
matched_finding.description: Throughout all experiments, participants are explicitly told 'not to confuse real and pseudo-letters' and given trial-by-trial feedback. Despite this, pseudo-to-real errors are markedly more common than real-to-pseudo errors, and this asymmetry is interpreted as driven by 'world knowledge.' However, the task structure itself (more real letters in displays and response options in Experiments 1–2; explicit knowledge that letters come in 'standard' and 'mirrored' forms) could generate a response-level bias independent of any memory process. The authors argue against a response bias because 'the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias,' but no formal model of response bias (e.g., signal detection theory decomposing d' and criterion) is applied to separate memory sensitivity from response criterion. Signal detection analysis could distinguish whether the effect reflects changes in memory representation versus changes in decision threshold, but this analysis is absent.
matched_finding.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Creates internal contradiction detectable within the paper
ground_truth.description: Changed stimulus size from 1.16° to 0.05° — below visual acuity threshold, contradicts successful task performance reported in results

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: FTT 'inhibit'→'facilitate' reverses prediction — must know FTT's actual prediction about similarity
ground_truth.original_snippet: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should inhibit false memories
ground_truth.modified_snippet: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories
ground_truth.description: Reversed FTT prediction from 'inhibit' to 'facilitate' — paper no longer differentiates its account from FTT; removes key theoretical contribution

matched_finding.subcategory: mischaracterization of fuzzy trace theory's prediction about similarity
matched_finding.description: The authors argue that FTT (fuzzy trace theory) 'predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories' and then dismiss FTT because illusions are abundant despite similarity. However, FTT's prediction that similarity facilitates false memories specifically refers to gist-level or semantic similarity (e.g., 'sleep' and 'dream' share semantic gist), not low-level visual/perceptual similarity. The physical mirror-reversal that distinguishes pseudo-letters from real letters would, under FTT, represent a difference at the verbatim level precisely captured by the gist representation 'letter + mirrored.' The dismissal of FTT based on a conflation of visual similarity with gist similarity is theoretically inaccurate and undermines the validity of the theoretical comparison.
matched_finding.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant. Therefore, it seems that FTT cannot accurately account for the occurrence of this type of memory illusions in STM.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Training exclusion dropped from Exps 2-4 without stated justification — must notice cross-experiment procedural change
ground_truth.original_snippet: Since only 10% of participants were excluded from participating in the main experiment based on the training scores, the training procedure was not part of Experiments 2, 3 and 4 in order to not make the overall time on task too long.
ground_truth.description: Removed justification for dropping training/screening from Exps 2-4 — undisclosed procedural change; those experiments lack minimum-competence screening that Exp 1 had

matched_finding.subcategory: training criterion applied only to Experiment 1 creates non-comparable participant populations
matched_finding.description: Experiment 1 required participants to score above 75% on a cued change detection training task before proceeding, specifically to 'ensure that all participants were motivated, and possessed a minimal proficiency at visual memory tasks.' This selection criterion is absent from Experiments 2–4. Experiment 2 explicitly recruited first-year psychology students via course enrollment with no performance screening. The absence of equivalent eligibility criteria means the participant populations are not comparable across experiments, and the replication logic (each experiment confirming prior results) is weakened by systematic differences in participant ability and motivation.
matched_finding.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training... [Experiment 2:] The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: 23+5=28 doesn't equal stated N=40 — arithmetic contradiction
ground_truth.original_snippet: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded)
ground_truth.modified_snippet: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)
ground_truth.description: Changed exclusions from 17 to 5 — hides 42.5% attrition rate (17/40); true rate raises concerns about selective retention of overconfident responders; 23+5=28 doesn't equal 40

matched_finding.description: The Methods section states 45 participants began training, 5 were excluded, leaving 40 for the main experiment. The Analysis section then reports that 5 further participants were excluded for low high-confidence trials, yielding 23 included participants. However, 40 − 5 = 35, not 23. Twelve participants are entirely unaccounted for with no explanation provided. This unexplained attrition represents 30% of the post-training sample and raises serious concerns about selective reporting or undisclosed exclusion criteria.
matched_finding.quote: The remaining 40 participants...Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)
